title: Inflight Request Quota Allocator — Design Scrub and Decisions
content:
Meeting: Inflight Request Quota Allocator — design scrub
Date: 2026-02-20 10:00–11:30 PT
Location: Zoom + #serving-runtime
Attendees: Anjali Rao (owner), Marcus Lin, Sofia Martinez, Elliot Park, Priya Desai, Darren Chu

Objective:
- Review RFC draft for a global "inflight request quota allocator" that provides per-tenant admission control to protect SLOs during bursts and noisy neighbors.
- Surface corner cases, operational signals, and rollout plan for Dedicated and Hosted API.

Agenda:
1) Quick recap of problem statement and goals (Anjali) — 10m
2) Architecture walkthrough and alternatives (Marcus) — 30m
3) Operational signals & metrics (Sofia) — 15m
4) Failure modes and graceful degradation (Elliot & Priya) — 20m
5) Rollout plan, canary criteria, and action items (All) — 15m

Summary of problem:
- Spiky request patterns (short-lived fanout, client retries) periodically push certain model variants past latency SLOs. Existing autoscaling is too slow for small bursts and caching helps only if prefix reuse exists.
- Need admission controls that: (a) prevent tail-latency amplification when node resources saturate, (b) allow controlled bursts for high-priority tenants, (c) operate across Dedicated/Hosted/private deployments with minimal customer config.

Design proposal (high level):
- Token-based inflight quota allocator (global control plane config + local fast-path):
  - Each tenant has a token bucket representing allowed concurrent inflight work (measured in "inflight units"). An inflight unit approximates expected GPU work — initial mapping: 1 inflight unit ~= 1 request of default sequence length (256 tokens) on a baseline model.
  - Token refill is adaptive: refill rate = max( min_capacity, EWMA(request_size) * baseline_rate_factor ). This lets heavy-request tenants have lower refill density while bursty small requests can be allowed in short windows.
  - Priority tiers: system, enterprise, standard. Higher tiers get separate burst credits and softer decay windows.
  - Elastic burst credits: tenants accumulate short-term burst tokens up to a capped allowance; credits decay over a configurable sliding window (default 5m).
  - Local fast-path: each node maintains a small local permit cache (LRU) keyed by tenant -> cached tokens to allow sub-ms admission without control-plane roundtrip. Global counters reconcile asynchronously.
  - Admission outcomes: allow, queue-with-timeout (soft queue), reject-with-backoff (hard). Soft queueing is bounded and used only for standard-tier; enterprise-tier gets higher soft-queue time and higher burst cap.

Alternatives reviewed and tradeoffs:
- Centralized rate-limiter (single-store tokens): simple but introduces a synchronous hop and single-point latency increase. Rejected due to tail amplification in high-throughput paths.
- Per-node static concurrency caps per tenant: trivial but inefficient for multi-node spread; requires heavy scheduling coordination and leads to wasted headroom.
- Cost-aware request scoring (est. GPU time per request) without tokens: promising but requires accurate estimator and still needs an admission knob; considered as future refinement to replace heuristic inflight units.

Key decisions reached (consensus):
1) Implement a hybrid token-bucket with local fast-path + global reconciliation. Rationale: best SLO protection with low tail effect.
2) Use inflight units as initial abstraction (coarse-grained, simple mapping) and plan to iterate to model-cost estimators (telemetry-driven) in Q3.
3) Default token decay window 5m, burst cap = 3x steady-state allowance for standard tier; enterprise gets 8x cap. Tunable via account config on Dedicated.
4) Soft queuing allowed but must be limited: max soft-queue latency default 300ms for standard, 1s for enterprise. After soft queue timeout, requests get polite reject (429) with Retry-After.
5) Local cache TTL for permits: 250ms with lease-renew protocol. This keeps local latency sub-ms while reconciling every ~2–3s.

Operational signals & metrics to add (Sofia):
- inflight_units_in_use{tenant} (gauge)
- token_refill_rate{tenant} (gauge)
- burst_credits{tenant} (gauge)
- admission_outcome{allow,soft_queue,reject} (counter)
- soft_queue_latency_histogram
- token_reconciliation_lag (gauge)
- observed_model_time_per_request_estimate (summary)

Failure modes & mitigations (Elliot/Priya):
- Local cache divergence causes brief over-allocation: mitigated by conservative local lease size and global reconciliation backpressure. If global detects >5% oversubscribe over 30s, trigger temporary stricter refill factor globally.
- Redis or control-plane store outage: fallback to per-node degraded mode with stricter static caps per tenant and emit alerts. Circuit-breaker TTL of 60s before aggressive caps.
- Latency amplification when many tenants burst: prefer graceful degradation by prioritizing enterprise/system tiers and issuing polite 429s for standard tier; also expose per-tenant telemetry to CS for debugging.
- Hot-tenant migration across nodes: ensure transfer of local cached permits via short-lived token handoff when session affinity changes; fallback is to drop local cache and re-acquire tokens from global store.

Compatibility & rollout notes:
- Hosted API: default enforcement enabled for new tenants; existing high-traffic tenants flagged for opt-in during canary wave.
- Dedicated: enforcement off by default; turn on per-customer after ops runbook and a 2-week soak in staging. Provide config UI in Console under "Routing & Throttling".
- Private (on-prem): simple config template + migration playbook; local store requirement documented (Redis recommended or embedded in-runtime for air-gapped installs).

Canary plan and success criteria:
- Canary cohort: 10 low-risk tenants across 2 regions (us-west1 + eu-west1) with small steady-state traffic and known request profiles.
- Canary duration: 2 weeks, with staged ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 100% traffic diverted to quota allocator by week 2.
- Success metrics:
  - no more than 1% increase in 95th pct latency across cohort (slo guardrail)
  - reduction in node-level tail latencies during bursts (95th latency improvement vs baseline)
  - admission_reject_rate < 0.5% overall and <2% for standard-tier tenants
  - token_reconciliation_lag median < 500ms

Open questions & follow-ups:
- How to map inflight units to heterogeneous hardware classes (A100 vs L40 vs TPU variants)? Action: Marcus to prototype a cost-normalized mapping table and report by 2026-03-05.
- Should we expose a tenant-level "burst budget" control in the API vs console only? Short-term: console only. CS/solutions to evaluate API for partners. Action: Priya to sync with Solutions Eng by 2026-02-28.
- Billing implications for burst credits (if a tenant consumes > cap): classification for chargebacks? Action: Darren to loop in FinOps and provide proposal by 2026-03-10 (JIRA INF-4837).

Action items (owners + due dates):
- Marcus: prototype hardware-normalized inflight-unit mapping + microbench results (2026-03-05)
- Sofia: extend telemetry pipeline to include token_reconciliation_lag and admission_outcome counters (2026-03-03)
- Elliot: draft degraded-mode runbook for Redis/control-plane outage (2026-02-27)
- Priya: coordinate Solutions Eng and CS on console UX & API decision (2026-02-28)
- Darren: FinOps billing impact write-up and JIRA ticket (INF-4837) (2026-03-10)
- Anjali: update RFC with decisions and rollout plan, attach canary cohort list, and open implementation epic (2026-02-24)

Notes & rationale excerpts (for RFC):
- We intentionally prefer a hybrid (local cache + global store) because fully centralized token checks cause synchronous hop penalties that increase tail latencies — invariants observed during load runs in Q4 2025.
- Soft queueing is a pragmatic middle ground: it reduces rejected work while keeping latency bounds; we must be conservative with default timeouts to avoid head-of-line blocking.

Appendix: quick sketch of local permit flow (text):
1) Request arrives on node -> check local permit cache for tenant. If cached tokens available, decrement and immediately proceed.
2) If local tokens exhausted, async probe to local allocator that attempts to acquire lease (fast path) from global store; if probe delays >18ms and request is low-priority, enter short soft-queue; else politely reject.
3) Background reconciler refreshes local cache every 2–3s and emits reconciliation metrics.

Next meeting: follow-up design review after Marcus prototype + Sofia telemetry (tentative 2026-03-09).

Document history:
- 2026-02-20: initial scrub and decisions (this doc)
- 2026-02-21: minor edits from Elliot and Sofia (clarified soft-queue rules)

End of notes.
